title: When does rotor cant pay on a small quadrotor co-designed with its motors and controller?
lede: research programme: fixed rotor cant on a co-designed quadrotor; cant cuts attitude error by 4.2–5.3° under INDI, geometric and PID control (10 of 10 seeds) and still wins every seed in RotorPy with canted rotors; in position hold it cuts yaw error 5–8°; on a rigid frame its side force hurts one horizontal axis (1.9–3.4× the other) whichever side the centre of pressure is on; a feed-forward from the commanded torque evens the axes but adds a rare divergence; one from the attitude integrator alone, retrained, evens them with no divergence when the integrator carries the gust torque, and runs away if bolted onto an untuned design; a linear stability test of the full loop catches every divergence (none among 2,688 flights it calls stable) and shows the optimiser tuned the integrator gain onto the stability boundary, so keep ki at about 0.8× its ceiling; the flights it calls unstable that hold on are contained by the 20° tilt-command limit, not the integrator clip, and diverge once that limit is raised; trained with that margin as a constraint, the designs lose 0.7% in cost and stop diverging when the tilt limit is raised to 45° (0 of 384 flights against 13)
summary: An open research programme (target IEEE RA-L) on when a fixed rotor cant angle pays on a small quadrotor once arm, propeller, motor headroom and attitude controller are designed with it. Milestone 1 found that the torque limits of seven earlier simulated steps understated yaw authority by 2× to 2.8×; cant still beat no cant by 4.8° RMS. Milestone 2 makes roll, pitch and yaw share one thrust polytope through an attitude-priority mixer (as PX4 and Betaflight do) and puts a price on hover power. Without cant the tuned vehicle saturates roll and pitch on 97% of steps and yaw gets nothing; cant's paired advantage grows to 6.08° (SD 0.28, 5 of 5 seeds). Pricing power at 0.3° per 100 W cuts hover power 4–7× for under 0.5° of error, but the chosen cant stays at 28–37° in 9 of 10 seed-arms (best of three CMA-ES starts), refuting the hypothesis of a small 5–20° optimum; cant still wins the priced objective in 5 of 5 seeds at 0.3 and 4 of 5 at 1° per 100 W. Single-start CMA-ES is unreliable on the polytope (2 of 5 seeds fell to low cant). Milestone 4 asks whether cant only patches a weak controller: with incremental nonlinear dynamic inversion (INDI) or geometric SO(3) attitude control co-designed in place of PID (10 seeds, three CMA-ES starts each), cant still wins by 4.18° (INDI), 4.88° (geometric) and 5.27° (PID) in 10 of 10 seeds, and INDI without cant is 4.02° worse than PID with cant in 10 of 10. INDI narrows the gap by 1.1° and mostly steadies the uncanted vehicle; the chosen cant stays at a 34–35° median under every law. Simulated; TWR fixed at 2; the power price is a swept modelling choice; mass, cost and motor fits and plant ranges are inherited assumptions; no hardware. Milestone 6 adds position hold with the side force derived from the allocation (sinα / (L cosα − κ sinα) per unit roll torque, √2 smaller than an earlier study used), 6 s episodes and a 3 m/s wind step. Cant cuts yaw error by 4.7° in 6 of 6 seeds and does not buy position. Whether the side force costs position depends on the sign of the gust's disturbance torque, that is, on where the centre of pressure sits. Under the inherited sign the force opposes the drag and costs nothing (0.96×); flipped, it costs 1.21×, past the hypothesis's 20% line (re-scored, not retrained). Cant still wins the composite in 4 of 6 and 6 of 6 seeds. Milestone 6b derives the rigid-frame case: drag at a centre of pressure above or below the centre of mass gives opposite roll and pitch torque signs, which the inherited model did not have. Retrained under either geometry (6 seeds), the side force opposes the drag on one horizontal axis and adds to it on the other: late-window position error on the hurt axis is 1.9–3.4× the other axis. The typical design loses only 3% overall (median), but one seed in six diverges on 1–2 of 64 episodes. Cant still cuts yaw error by 5.1–7.7° (6 of 6) and wins the composite in 5 and 6 of 6 seeds. The translation model and the centre-of-pressure lever are inherited and assumed (lever swept 0–2×). Milestone 5 re-scores the 60 milestone-4 designs, not retuned, in RotorPy with a canted-rotor wrench, motor-speed dynamics and rotor aerodynamics scaled from its Hummingbird model. Cant still wins in 10 of 10 seeds for every law under RotorPy aerodynamics (3.1–5.8°), and the six law × cant arms keep their order (ρ 0.94–1.00; ρ 0.88–0.91 over all 60 designs against 0.95–0.97 for the stylised simulator against itself). The pre-registered top-ten test fails (ρ 0.20–0.30), but the top ten are tied and the stylised simulator scores only 0.26 against itself on fresh episodes. The stylised model is 1–2° optimistic, most for INDI. Milestone 7 lets the position loop predict the side force from its own commanded torque and lean against it (no new sensor): retrained with it, the one-axis penalty disappears (hurt/helped 1.08–1.10 against 1.91–3.41), but the term closes a loop through the motor lag that diverges on a few held-out episodes when its filter is fast (16% of episodes at 0.2 s on unretrained designs, 1.3% at 1 s), so the composite is unchanged above and worse below (J −0.33). Cant still beats no cant by 5–7° of yaw in 6 of 6 seeds. Milestone 7b feeds forward only the attitude integrator’s torque, so the proportional and derivative path no longer closes a fast loop. Retrained with it on a frame whose centre of pressure is above the centre of mass, no held-out episode diverges at the design wind (hurt/helped 0.83; 2.06 with it switched off) and fewer do out of distribution (15 against 23 of 384); below, the designs barely use their integrator (ki/kp 0.05–0.28 s−1 against 3.7–12.6) and the term is nearly inert (ratio 2.04 against 3.01) but harmless. Added to milestone 6b’s integrator-heavy designs without retraining it diverges on 23% of episodes even with no gust torque: it must come with a retune. Cant still cuts yaw error 5–8° in 6 of 6 seeds. Milestone 7c linearises the full attitude-plus-position loop (11 states, motor lag, one-step-old measurements, either feed-forward; matched to the simulator to 10−3) and tests it on 84 design-conditions × 64 held-out flights. It is a necessary test: no flight it calls stable at its own plant diverged (0 of 2,688 with the integrator feed-forward or none; 1 of 758 with the commanded-torque one), but 300 flights it calls unstable held on (accuracy 0.90 against 0.95 predicted). The retrained designs’ ki/kp (3.7–4.4 s−1) sits at 0.88–1.11× the linear ceiling; the bolted-on ones at 2.3–3.4×. New designs at 0.8× their ceiling never diverge; at 1.25× the slow instability (0.5–0.7 s−1) stays bounded. Linearised about hover; the clips where divergence happens are outside the model. Milestone 7d asks what contains those unstable flights: not the attitude integrator’s clip (never reached; removing it changes no count) and not the 6 s flight length (the linear model kills 60% of them within 6 s from their initial offset alone; none diverges in 18 s flights). The 20° tilt-command limit does: raised to 45–59° (post hoc), 83–88% of the 1.25× designs’ 18 s flights diverge, close to the 96% the model calls unstable, and designs tuned onto the ceiling lose 3–4%; at 0.8× none diverges at any limit. Milestone 7e trains with the margin as a CMA-ES constraint (ki ≤ 0.8× ceiling at every plant corner): the centre-of-pressure-above designs land on it and lose 0.011 in held-out cost (about 0.7%); at a 45–59° tilt limit they diverge on 0 of 384 flights against 13 for the unconstrained designs, and at twice the trained lever on 4 against 15. With the centre of pressure below the constraint barely binds and changes nothing.
